page_title: Building Blockchain in Go. Part 2: Proof-of-Work - Going the distance

summary.title: Building Blockchain in Go. Part 2: Proof-of-Work
summary.one_liner: You learn how proof-of-work (Hashcash-style hashing with a nonce and a difficulty target) makes adding blocks costly, and how to implement mining and validation in Go.
takeaways: Proof-of-work makes adding blocks expensive: a miner must find a nonce whose SHA-256 hash, over block data plus nonce, falls below a target.
Hashcash is a brute-force algorithm: increment a counter, hash the combined data, and check the result against a requirement until it is met.
The target is 1 shifted left by 256 minus targetBits; a hash is valid when, read as a big integer, it is less than the target.
Verifying a proof is cheap: recompute one hash using the stored nonce and compare it with the target.
The article leaves persistence, wallets, transactions and consensus for later parts.
summary.summary: The article is the second part of a series building a toy blockchain in Go. It explains hashing properties, the Hashcash proof-of-work scheme used by Bitcoin, and why the difficulty target is needed. It then implements a ProofOfWork struct with a target, data preparation, a mining loop over nonces with SHA-256, and a Validate method, and shows sample output where each block hash begins with three zero bytes. It ends by noting that persistence, wallets, transactions and consensus are left for future articles.
